title: The Summer Nobody in Cornwall Would Lend Boulton and Watt £500
dek: In 1778 the steam-engine partnership had cost far more than it had earned, and Matthew Boulton chose to borrow against the engines rather than stop.

story.event: The 1778 cash crisis: borrowing against the engine royalties instead of stopping payment
story.summary: In the summer of 1778, with the steam-engine business so far only a cost, Boulton's bank shaken and Cornish miners slow to pay, James Watt reported from Redruth that no one would lend the firm £500 on its engines, and Boulton's partner Fothergill urged him to stop payment. Boulton instead borrowed £7,000 from a merchant named Wiss against an annuity and carried a £14,000 bank debt secured on the engine royalties, while Watt insisted on signed terms of a third of the coal saved. The engine business paid Watt a real profit only around 1785 to 1787, and Boulton remained in debt for years after.
paragraphs: In early July 1778 James Watt, lodging at Redruth in Cornwall's mining country, wrote to his partner Matthew Boulton in Birmingham. Boulton had asked him to raise money from the Cornish bankers. Watt had tried. The mine owners had so little faith in the new engine, he reported, that he knew nobody who would lend them £500 on a mortgage of it.

Watt's engine, which burned far less coal than the old Newcomen type, had been at work since 1776, and engines were going up at Cornish mines. But so far the engine business had only cost money. Boulton paid for tools, workshops and Watt's living; the miners would not pay until their engines were working. That July a junior partner of Boulton's London bank absconded, and the Bank of England refused some of his bills. John Fothergill, Boulton's partner in the hardware trade, kept writing that bankruptcy was inevitable and urged him to stop payment. Watt suggested taking the ironmaster John Wilkinson in as a partner.

Boulton chose to borrow instead. Over the following months he raised £7,000 from a merchant named Wiss, repaid as an annuity secured on engine contracts, and the bankers Lowe, Vere and Williams carried £14,000 on a mortgage of the engine royalties, with Watt personally bound. In August Watt reported the Chacewater engine running well: "our capital card". He also refused to draw another engine until its terms were signed: the firm would take a third of the value of the coal saved, later counted by a locked meter on the beam. That way, he told Boulton, they would get "enough to keep us out of jail, in continual apprehension of which I live at present."

Relief came slowly. By one historian's count, engines erected up to the end of 1782 had brought in a net £3,724, against £9,878 due had all been working. Watt drew his living from the hardware firm until 1785, and only in 1787 was he credited £4,000 from the engines. Boulton, who had sold an estate from his wife's inheritance and mortgaged much of his father's property, wrote in 1788 of groaning under "a load of debt and annuities". The Cornish miners argued over payments until the patent ran out in 1800.

quote.text: He that resteth upon gains certain, shall hardly grow to great riches; and he that puts all upon adventures, doth oftentimes break and come to poverty: it is good, therefore, to guard adventures with certainties, that may uphold losses.
quote.source_title: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Project Gutenberg eBook #575
quote.connection: Bacon names the risk Boulton was running. He had put almost everything on the engine, and the hardware trade meant to steady it was itself losing money. That the firm came through does not prove Bacon wrong, and Watt's dread of jail suggests he wished for more certainty too.

reflection: Watt and Boulton looked at the same ledger and felt it differently. Watt, by his own letters, lived in fear of the debt; Boulton kept borrowing and kept the works open. Neither was simply right. The fear made Watt insist on terms in writing, and the nerve kept the firm alive long enough for those terms to pay.

Bacon would ask what certainty was holding up the adventure. When you weigh how much more of yourself to put into your work, it helps to know what is quietly carrying the risk: savings, a salary, your health, the patience of the people at home. Name it, and do not spend it without saying so.
invitation: Write down the one certainty that holds up your riskiest piece of work, whether savings, a salary or someone's patience. Under it, write the line you will not cross with it this year.

sources.title: Lives of Boulton and Watt, Principally from the Original Soho MSS. (1865)
sources.publisher: Samuel Smiles; John Murray, London; Project Gutenberg eBook #52069
sources.supports: Partnership terms dated from 1 June 1775 for 25 years; Watt at Redruth from June 1778; the engine business so far only an outlay; miners refusing to pay until engines were complete; Watt's letters of 2 and 8 July 1778 that a Cornish loan was impossible and no one would advance £500 on a mortgage of the engine; Watt's suggestion of Wilkinson as partner; Fothergill's letters that bankruptcy was inevitable and his advice to stop payment; £7,000 raised from Mr Wiss on an annuity and £14,000 advanced by Lowe, Vere and Williams on a mortgage of the engine royalties; Watt's August 1778 letters on Chacewater and Tingtang and 'our capital card'; Watt's letter of 29 August 1778 refusing to draw engines without signed terms and 'enough to keep us out of jail, in continual apprehension of which I live at present'; the one-third of fuel saved and the counter; no division of engine profits until after 1785; £4,000 transferred to Watt's account in December 1787; Boulton's 1788 letter on 'a load of debt and annuities'; disputes with the Cornish miners ending only with the patent.

sources.title: Capital and Steam-Power, 1750–1800: Capitalization of the Firm of Boulton & Watt (John Lord, 1923)
sources.publisher: The Hopkin Thomas Project (online edition of John Lord's study)
sources.supports: First engines ready in 1776 (Wilkinson's Broseley works and Bloomfield Colliery); payment from the saving in coal divided two to one; Watt credited £330 a year until the business paid; Fothergill refusing a share of the engine business; Boulton's wife's £28,000 and the sale of an estate for £15,000, and his father's property sold or mortgaged; the July 1778 absconding of Jennings of Lowe, Vere, Williams & Jennings and the Bank of England refusing Boulton's bills; Watt's 8 July 1778 letter on the £500 mortgage; Watt's suggestion of Wilkinson as third partner; the £7,000 Wiss annuity arranged towards the end of 1778; the £14,000 owed to Lowe, Vere with Watt's personal bond; net engine income of £3,724 to the end of 1782 against £9,878 due; Watt ceasing to draw his £330 in 1785 and being credited £4,000 in 1787; the hardware firm's losses of £11,000 over 1762–1780.

sources.title: Boulton, Matthew (Dictionary of National Biography, 1885–1900, volume 6)
sources.publisher: Wikisource (H. T. W. [Henry Trueman Wright Wood], 1886)
sources.supports: Boulton took Roebuck's share of the engine patent and went into partnership with Watt; the act of parliament extending the patent; Boulton put in all his own capital and all he could raise and brought himself to the verge of bankruptcy before the engine was a commercial success; Smiles dating Watt's first profit from the engine to 1787, with Boulton clearing his liabilities later still.

research_notes: The slate's episode (1776, 'years of losses') was narrowed to one documented moment inside those years: the cash crisis of summer and autumn 1778, which both Smiles (1865, from the Soho manuscripts) and John Lord (1923, from the Tew and Tangye manuscripts) describe letter by letter. Wording differences between the two transcriptions: Watt's 8 July 1778 letter reads 'no one I have conversed with would advance us 500l. on a mortgage of it' in Smiles and 'none I have conversed with would advance us £500' in Lord, and his line about Wilkinson reads 'run ashore' in Smiles and 'run on shore' in Lord; the story paraphrases both rather than quote either. Timing of the loans: Smiles narrates the £7,000 Wiss annuity and the £14,000 bank advance straight after the July crisis; Lord dates the Wiss negotiation to the end of 1778 (Wiss's letter of 7 November 1778); the story says 'over the following months'. Lord describes the £14,000 as a debt to Lowe, Vere for which Watt gave personal bonds; Smiles as an advance on a mortgage of the royalties; the story combines the two consistently. Payment terms: Smiles says the first Cornish engines were put up without agreed terms and the one-third rule was formalised in 1778; Lord says the terms were fixed from the beginning and calls Smiles 'scarcely accurate'; the story says only that Watt refused to draw new engines until terms were signed, which both support. Profit timing (outcome figure): Smiles says no engine profits were divided until after 1785 and Watt was free of the bank debt by 1787; Lord gives net engine income to end-1782 of £3,724 against £9,878 due, Watt ceasing to draw £330 a year in 1785 and £4,000 credited in 1787; the DNB (1886) says Smiles dates Watt's first profit to 1787 and Boulton's later. Lord also quotes Watt in July 1782 putting the 'clear income' of the engine business above £3,000 a year, which suggests gross income was growing while debts absorbed it; the story uses the conservative markers (1785 and 1787) and attributes the 1782 net figure to 'one historian's count' (Lord). 'Burned far less coal' is kept general: Smiles says about one-third the consumption at Chacewater, and figures for the fully developed engine vary. Boulton's hardware partner is named as John Fothergill. The Lord text online contains OCR errors (dropped £ signs, one '1788' that should read 1778); figures were checked for consistency with Smiles where both give them.
